details:
**The Phenomenology of Spirit**
Hegel's 1807 masterwork, which traces the development of consciousness through a series of "shapes," from "sense-certainty" and "perception" (Wahrnehmung) through self-consciousness and reason, up to Spirit (Geist) and finally "Absolute Knowing." It is often compared to a Bildungsroman and is the most common title giveaway.

**Master-slave (lord-bondsman) dialectic**
A famous passage in the Phenomenology's section on the "Independence and Dependence of Self-Consciousness." Two self-conscious beings, each seeking recognition from the other, engage in a "struggle to the death"; one submits and becomes the bondsman, but through labor the bondsman ultimately gains a truer self-consciousness than the lord. The idea influenced Marx, Sartre, and many others.

**Dialectic ("thesis, antithesis, synthesis")**
Hegel's method, in which a concept generates its own contradiction and the two are resolved into a higher concept that preserves both. The triad "thesis, antithesis, synthesis" is a popular oversimplification (Hegel's own terms are closer to abstract, negative, and concrete), but quizbowl questions use it constantly as a giveaway.

**Aufhebung (sublation)**
Hegel's term for how a contradiction is overcome, which means both "to cancel or abolish" and "to preserve or lift up." In the Science of Logic, pure Being and pure Nothing are sublated into Becoming, which then passes into Determinate Being.

**Alexandre Kojève**
The Russian-born French philosopher whose lectures on the Phenomenology in Paris in the 1930s, published as Introduction to the Reading of Hegel, emphasized the master-slave dialectic and the "end of history." They shaped a generation of French thinkers.

**Elements of the Philosophy of Right**
Hegel's 1820 political treatise, which divides "right" into three spheres: abstract right (property and contracts), morality, and ethical life (Sittlichkeit), which itself consists of the family, civil society, and the state. Its preface says that "philosophy is its own time comprehended in thoughts," declares "what is rational is actual and what is actual is rational," and attacks Jakob Fries for his part in the Wartburg Festival.

**Owl of Minerva**
From the preface to the Philosophy of Right: "the owl of Minerva spreads its wings only with the falling of dusk," after philosophy "paints its grey in grey." The image means that philosophy can only understand an era after it has already passed. Andrew Cutrofello titled a book The Owl at Dawn as a "sequel" to Hegel.

**Science of Logic**
Hegel's major work of logic and metaphysics (1812–16), divided into the doctrines of Being, Essence, and Concept (Notion), and into objective and subjective logic. It begins with pure Being, which is indistinguishable from pure Nothing, and treats quality (determinateness), quantity (magnitude), and measure; a shorter version forms the first part of his Encyclopedia of the Philosophical Sciences.

**Geist (Spirit) and the world-spirit**
Hegel's central concept of Spirit, a collective, developing consciousness. History is the process by which the world-spirit (Weltgeist) comes to know itself, working through national spirits (Volksgeister) and "great men" in what he called the "cunning of reason." He is also associated with the term Zeitgeist ("spirit of the age").

**Lectures on the Philosophy of History**
Hegel's lectures arguing that "reason is the substance of the universe" and that world history is the progress of the consciousness of freedom. Oriental despotism knew only one person as free, the Greeks and Romans some, and the Germanic world all. He infamously said Africa "is no historical part of the World," calling it "Unhistorical, Undeveloped Spirit."

**Young (Left) Hegelians and Right Hegelians**
After Hegel's death his followers split. The Young or Left Hegelians, including Ludwig Feuerbach, Bruno Bauer, and David Strauss, gave his ideas a radical and secular turn, while Right Hegelians such as Karl Daub and Johann Philipp Gabler stressed religion and the state.

**Karl Marx "standing Hegel on his head"**
Marx said that in Hegel the dialectic was "standing on its head" and had to be turned right side up. Marx kept Hegel's dialectical view of history but replaced his idealism with materialism, producing what became known as dialectical materialism.

**Antigone**
Hegel used Sophocles's Antigone in the Phenomenology to illustrate the clash between divine law (family duty, the "unwritten and infallible law of the gods") and human law (the state). He saw tragedy as a collision between two legitimate ethical powers.

**Absolute idealism**
Hegel's philosophical system, developed in dialogue with Friedrich Schelling and built on Kant and Fichte. It holds that reality is ultimately the self-unfolding of rational Spirit, so that "the real is rational and the rational is real."

**The state and critics like Karl Popper**
Hegel called the state "the march of God on earth" and the "actually existing, realized moral life," and he was seen as glorifying the Prussian state. Karl Popper, in The Open Society and Its Enemies, attacked him as a forerunner of modern totalitarianism.
